documents.subject: Portion of a confidential settlement-purpose statement discussing male comparator reporters' salaries relative to Martha Hamilton's at The Washington Post
documents.date: 2002 or later (text references salary snapshots through 2002 and 'As of September 1, 2002')

pages.transcript:
CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES
PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES

Grimaldi received a high salary from the Seattle Times, his previous employer - more than the salary of Hamilton at The Post at that time. Therefore, Grimaldi's starting salary was substantially more than the salary of Hamilton at that time.

The differential between the salary of Grimaldi and the salaries of Mayer and Skrzycki is due in part to Grimaldi's high starting salary, which reflects The Post's desire to hire him away from the Seattle Times.

Blaine Harden

Blaine Harden does not appear on any of the relevant salary snapshots and was never a reporter in Financial News.

David Hilzenrath

David Hilzenrath was paid slightly less than Hamilton on the 1993, 1995 and 1996 salary snapshots and similarly to Hamilton on the 1994 and 1997 salary snapshots. Hilzenrath was paid slightly more than Hamilton on the 1998 and 1999 salary snapshots, more than Hamilton on the 2000 salary snapshot and substantially more than Hamilton on the 2001 and 2002 salary snapshots.

Hilzenrath was paid similarly to Mayer on the 1995 to 1998 salary snapshots, slightly less than Mayer on the 1999 salary snapshot and slightly more than Mayer on the 2000 to 2002 salary snapshots.

Experience and Education
Hilzenrath came to The Post in the late 1980s as a summer intern in National News. In 1987, he became a reporter in Metro/City, moving to Real Estate in 1988, and to Financial News in 1992. Prior to starting at The Post, Hilzenrath worked as an intern reporter at the Providence Journal and as an intern at WBZ-TV News. Hilzenrath is a graduate of Harvard University.

Starting Salary
Upon becoming a reporter at The Post, Hilzenrath received approximately a 12 percent increase over his prior salary as a Washington Post intern. His starting salary was substantially less than the salaries of Hamilton and Mayer at that time.

Salary History
As of September 1, 2002, Hilzenrath had received 13 merit increases - all of which he received as a reporter in Real Estate or Financial News. He received these merit increases in the following years: 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994, 1997, 1998, 2000, 2001 and 2002. In 2000, in response to a competing job offer, Hilzenrath was given a roughly 10 percent salary increase and was put on the fast-track.

documents.title: Post Unit News No. 99 - 'Discrimination at The Post: PAY GAPS WIDEN'
documents.subject: Washington/Baltimore Newspaper Guild unit newsletter reporting widened race and sex pay gaps at The Washington Post, with reporter salary comparison table (1/86 vs. 9/87)
documents.notes: One mimeographed/printed union newsletter page, flagged 'Discrimination at The Post' and marked '-over-' at the bottom, so the comparison table continues on a verso page that is not in this batch. Photographed on a rattan chair with a binder clip at the right edge.

pages.transcript:
-Post Unit News-

Washington/Baltimore Newspaper Guild
No. 99        Date October 22, 1987

Discrimination at The Post

                            PAY GAPS WIDEN

The patterns of pay discrimination that have contributed over the years to low morale and wide gaps in the amount Washington Post managers are willing to pay their employees not only persist, but have widened significantly since management imposed its version of the contract in August.

If you needed a reason to understand why this contract is inadequate, here it is.

Last we looked, white males topped the salary scales in the best-paying jobs in many of the largest job categories at the Post. The news is this: despite the company's stated commitments to the hiring and nurturing of women and minorities, the practice of paying inequitably based on race and sex has not only continued--it's gotten worse.

For reporters--the largest single job category covered by the contract--the average salary for white males was $988.68 at the beginning of 1986. By September of 1987, that figure had jumped to $1,140.52.

Such a salary improvement is not the source of our complaints, however. The problem is that while white males were continuing to improve, females and blacks continued the slide away from parity.

The numbers compiled after the so-called impasse was declared in mid-August tell the story.

Across all classifications, white males average $332 more a week than black females, $204.39 more than white females and $230.66 more than black males.

Among reporters, the figures are reversed slightly, but the discrepancies remain just as stark. White male reporters, on the average, make $240.59 more a week than black females, a gap that is $43.24 wider than in January of 1986.

The gap has also grown by about $2 a week between white male and white female reporters and by about $15 a week between white male and black male reporters.

Among outside advertising salespersons, the gap also increased significantly. White males, on average, earned about $25 more a week than black males and black females in 1986, a disparity which has now increased to $96 weekly. White females in this classification earn on average $61.51 less than their male counterparts, up from a $43.03 average weekly difference in 1986.

And the gap among white men and white women who work as T-5 Data Programmers has opened dramatically, moving from an $8.33 average weekly difference in 1986 to an $86.07 average difference now.

There have been some improvements. Black females who are classified as managers, assistant managers, editors, deputy and associate editors have closed a more than $200 gap between their average salaries and salaries for white males.

But overall, the Post's record on equal pay for equal work sends a clear message to the rank and file at the Washington Post about which employees are valued at this company, and which are not.

These comparisons tell the story:

Reporters                                    1/86          9/87

White males                                 $988.68        $1,140.52
Black males                                  $920.46        $1,057.39
White females                                $859.37        $1,008.56
Black females                                $791.33           $ 899.33

                                -over-
